title: Botched Router Upgrade Grounds Nationwide Air Travel, Triggering Calls for Infrastructure Overhaul
snippet: A routine router installation by an FAA contractor caused a massive system overload that grounded U.S. flights nationwide, sparking massive travel delays and fierce debate on Capitol Hill over air traffic infrastructure.
content:
WASHINGTON — U.S. air travel is slowly recovering following an unprecedented system failure that grounded flights nationwide in the longest halt to domestic aviation since September 11, 2001. Federal officials traced the historic disruption to a botched routine router upgrade performed by a government contractor, prompting widespread frustration and mounting political scrutiny.

By Saturday night, airlines had canceled more than 6,400 U.S. flights and delayed over 8,000 others, according to flight-tracking data. The fallout followed Friday's chaotic five-hour ground stop, which saw more than 9,200 flights canceled. Although Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Administrator Bryan Bedford offered apologies and anticipated a return to normal schedules by late Sunday, tens of thousands of passengers remained stranded at airports across the country.

A System Overwhelmed by Data

The crisis began Friday afternoon when air traffic controllers experienced sudden instability across radar and communication systems. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy revealed Saturday that the issue stemmed from a remote facility in which defense contractor L3Harris was installing at least one updated router.

The installation triggered a catastrophic data flood, producing over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. The resulting overload impacted communications at 17 of the FAA’s 22 en-route traffic control centers, which direct high-altitude commercial flights across the country. "We're working to determine whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router?" Duffy said during a press conference.

L3Harris released a statement noting it takes the incident seriously and is fully assisting the FAA's investigation. Meanwhile, the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union, which represents FAA safety technicians, emphasized that its members were not involved in the third-party upgrade.

Infrastructure Strain and Political Fallout

The multi-day meltdown underscores ongoing vulnerabilities within a national air traffic system burdened by aging hardware, technological bottlenecks, and severe staffing shortages. In light of the crisis, Secretary Duffy urged Congress to approve $50 billion to modernize the aviation grid—a significant jump from his previous request of $30 billion.

The outage has also drawn swift bipartisan attention on Capitol Hill. House Speaker Mike Johnson indicated support for approving additional air traffic funding this year, while key lawmakers pledged rigorous congressional oversight. Representatives slated to helm the House Transportation Committee next year promised to hold both the administration and contractors accountable to ensure a failure of this magnitude does not happen again.
